title: Day 1: How to make a Quarto blog
text:
creating the blog
Creating the blog was actually fairly easy. All we need to do is open VScode and create a new project. Then, we select the Quarto blog and that’s it! The blog skeleton is created and we can now personalise it.

title: Day 1: How to make a Quarto blog
text:
blog structure
We will have one post for every day of the course, so five in total. What we need to do for this is have a “posts” folder where we will create a new folder for every day. There, we will write inside the index.qmd file, which contains the content of this post.

title: Day 1: How to make a Quarto blog
text:
publishing it on github
First, we create a new repository on github. Then:
git init
git add .
git commit -m "Initial blog"
git remote add origin https://github.com/<user>/<repo>.git
git branch -M main
git push -u origin main

title: Day 2: Pixi, quality control and containers
text: A problem with reproducible research is that different software versions and dependencies can lead to very different results. So how do we solve this?

title: Day 2: Pixi, quality control and containers
text:
Pixi
Pixi is an environment manager that we can run on all major operating systems. Pixi installs tools and dependencies in one project, so that others can reproduce the same results.
pixi init myproject -c conda-forge -c bioconda   # conda-forge first!
cd myproject
pixi add fastqc multiqc
pixi run fastqc --help

title: Day 2: Pixi, quality control and containers
text:
pixi file structure
But what are the files that we now have in the project? pixi.toml lists the channels, platforms and dependencies. pixi.lock records the exact versions of the dependencies and is not to be ever deleted!

title: Day 2: Pixi, quality control and containers
text:
quality control
In bioinformatics, quality control is a fundamental step to make sure that the data is of good quality. One way to do this is using FastQC, a tool that generates a report with quality metrics.
We ran fastqc on the samples and then used MultiQC to summarize the results in one report.

title: Day 2: Pixi, quality control and containers
text:
containers
Containers are built as container images that specify the operating system, dependencies, and software in an isolated environment. The container management tool then takes the images and build the container. These management tools can be run on all operating systems and it will run in all environments.
To download container images, we could use for example dockerhub or seqera.
We then used apptainer to get the image with apptainer pulland run the software inside the container with apptainer exec.:
apptainer pull fastqc_0.12.1.sif docker://biocontainers/fastqc:v0.11.9_cv8
apptainer exec fastqc_0.12.1.sif fastqc --version

title: Day 2: Pixi, quality control and containers
text:
running containers with sbatch
We can run apptainer containers as part of a batch job. Example:
#! /bin/bash -l
#SBATCH -A project_ID
#SBATCH -t 30:00
#SBATCH -n 1

apptainer exec container_image.sif fastqc -o . --noextract ../data/*fastq.gz

title: Day 4: nf-core pipelines
text: nf-core is a community built around nextflow, where people build nextflow pipelines on different bioinformatics data.

title: Day 4: nf-core pipelines
text:
why use nf-core?
When we want to analyse data, we can be pretty sure that a pipeline for that type of data probably already exists. So we can save time and effort by using an already validated pipeline, built and maintained by an expert. We also get all the benefits of nextflow, like reproducibility and portability.

title: Day 4: nf-core pipelines
text:
setup
So now all we have to do is to create a pixi environment containing nextflow and nf-core:
pixi init nextflow_test -c conda-forge -c bioconda
cd nextflow_test
pixi add nextflow nf-core

title: Day 4: nf-core pipelines
text:
test run
In this example, we will use the Sarek pipeline:
pixi run nextflow run nf-core/sarek -profile test --outdir sarek_test -c hpc2n.config
hpc2n.config is a configuration file that we need to run this pipeline on our cluster!

title: Day 4: nf-core pipelines
section: running nf-core pipeline on real data!
text:
running nf-core pipeline on real data!
We first made a samplesheet with the samples we wanted to analyse. Then we added it to the form on the nf-core launcher and ran it as a batch job:
pixi run nextflow run nf-core/rnaseq -r 3.26.0 -params-file nf-params.json -c hpc2n.config

title: Day 3: Workflow managers: Nextflow
text:
Running one script for every tool can become difficult, especially when the analyses are more complex. A workflow manager gathers the steps and runs them in the right order so that the pipeline becomes portable and reproducible. Once the pipeline is developed, all it takes is one command to start it.
Nextflow is one example of a workflow manager.
In nextflow, the scripts are turned into processes that are connected by channels that contain the data. Nextflow also performs checks on the processes and their input and output. So it can automatically resume execution at a point of failure without going back over the successful steps.
Here is how a nextflow script looks like. In this example, we take a string and split it into chunks, then we convert them to uppercase.
screen -S nextflow
pixi init -c conda-forge -c bioconda
pixi add nextflow

#!/usr/bin/env nextflow

params.greeting = 'Hello world!'

process SPLITLETTERS {
    input:
    val x

    output:
    path 'chunk_*'

    script:
    """
    printf '$x' | split -b 6 - chunk_
    """
}

process CONVERTTOUPPER {
    input:
    path y

    output:
    stdout

    script:
    """
    cat $y | tr '[a-z]' '[A-Z]'
    """
}

workflow {
    greeting_ch = Channel.of(params.greeting)
    letters_ch  = SPLITLETTERS(greeting_ch)
    results_ch  = CONVERTTOUPPER(letters_ch.flatten())
    results_ch.view { it }
}



pixi run nextflow run hello.nf
We should also periodically clean up the nextflow work directory. We can see the executions log and runtine information with:
pixi run nextflow log
Then we can clean up the work directory with:
pixi run nextflow clean -f

title: Day 5: ggplot
text:
In this last day of the course we addressed how to make plots, a fundamental step in data analysis. For this purpose, we used the R package ggplot2. The required parts to make a plot are the data (a dataframe), the aesthetics (what should be on the x and y axes) and a geom (what type of plot we want).
library(ggplot2)
library(palmerpenguins)


Attaching package: 'palmerpenguins'


The following objects are masked from 'package:datasets':

    penguins, penguins_raw

library(patchwork)

title: Day 5: ggplot
text:
example plot

ggplot(penguins, aes(x = flipper_length_mm, y = body_mass_g, colour = species)) +
  geom_point()

Warning: Removed 2 rows containing missing values or values outside the scale range
(`geom_point()`).









The nice thing is that we can save the plot as a variable and then add more to it! For example:

p <- ggplot(penguins)

p1 <- p + geom_bar(aes(x = species))
p2 <- p + geom_boxplot(aes(x = species, y = body_mass_g))

p1 + p2

Warning: Removed 2 rows containing non-finite outside the scale range
(`stat_boxplot()`).

title: Day 5: ggplot
text:
position
How we want to have the bars:

b <- ggplot(penguins, aes(x = factor(year), y = body_mass_g, fill = species)) + labs(x = "year")

(b + geom_bar(stat = "identity", position = "stack")) +
  (b + geom_bar(stat = "identity", position = "dodge")) +
  (b + geom_bar(stat = "identity", position = "fill")) +
  plot_layout(guides = "collect")

Warning: Removed 2 rows containing missing values or values outside the scale range
(`geom_bar()`).

title: Day 5: ggplot
text:
scales
Scales control how aesthetics are shown. For example:

ggplot(penguins, aes(flipper_length_mm, body_mass_g, colour = species)) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_colour_manual(name = "Species", values = c("#5BC0EB", "#FDE74C", "#9BC53D")) +
  scale_x_continuous(name = "Flipper length (mm)")

Warning: Removed 2 rows containing missing values or values outside the scale range
(`geom_point()`).

title: Day 5: ggplot
text:
facets
Facets allow us to split the data into subplots. For example, facet_wrap() splits a plot by a variable, and facet_grid() splits a plot by two variables:

ggplot(penguins, aes(flipper_length_mm, body_mass_g)) +
  geom_point() +
  facet_grid(island ~ year)

Warning: Removed 2 rows containing missing values or values outside the scale range
(`geom_point()`).

title: Day 5: ggplot
text:
themes
Themes control everything that is not data.

my_theme <- theme_bw() +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        legend.position = "top")

ggplot(penguins, aes(flipper_length_mm, body_mass_g, colour = species)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(title = "Bigger flippers, heavier penguins") +
  my_theme

Warning: Removed 2 rows containing missing values or values outside the scale range
(`geom_point()`).









Then we can save the plot as a pdf or png file:

ggsave("plot.png", p, height = 5, width = 7, units = "cm", dpi = 200)
